study_design_identified: Doctrinal-institutional policy case study with narrative literature review, statutory/regulatory analysis, and descriptive secondary federal administrative data synthesis (SNIS, SIGA Brasil/SIGPLAN, SIOP)
why_tool_chosen: The study is a hybrid legal-institutional and descriptive administrative-data analysis of Brazilian federal sanitation governance—combining constitutional/statutory interpretation (CF/88 Art. 23, Law 11.445/2007, Law 11.107/2005, EC 95/2016, MP 868/2018, PL 4.162/2019) and institutional mapping with descriptive secondary statistics from federal databases (SNIS, SIGA Brasil/SIGPLAN, SIOP). It has no randomized or quasi-experimental intervention comparator (excluding RoB 2 and ROBINS-I), no analytical cross-sectional or cohort statistical model (excluding JBI checklists), no primary qualitative fieldwork (excluding CASP and MMAT), and no systematic review protocol (excluding AMSTAR 2), making the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework the exact matching instrument.
overall_rating: Structured non-validated judgment: High methodological concern for empirical/causal inference (strong institutional and jurisdictional context, adequate legal/conceptual framing, weak sampling, measurement, coding, replication, confounding control, and causal identification)

domain_ratings.justification: Accurately identifies and discusses the core constitutional and statutory framework governing Brazilian basic sanitation and federalism (CF/88 Art. 23, Law 11.445/2007, Law 11.107/2005, Portaria 171/2014 PLANSAB, Portaria 141/2005, EC 95/2016, Lei de Responsabilidade Fiscal, MP 868/2018, PL 4.162/2019, and TCU Acórdão 593/2015). Rated adequate rather than strong because of minor citation inaccuracies (e.g., referring to Law 11.445/2007 as 'Lei n. 11.447/2007' on PDF p. 11) and attributing deadline postponements in Figura 1 generically to 'Decretos federais' without citing the specific decree numbers.

domain_ratings.justification: Clearly delineates the three-tier Brazilian federation (Union, states/Distrito Federal, and municipalities) and specifies exact institutional and demographic jurisdiction rules across federal bodies (Ministério das Cidades for municipalities >50,000 inhabitants, metropolitan regions, RIDEs, and consortia >150,000; FUNASA for municipalities <50,000 inhabitants, quilombos, and rural settlements; Ministério da Saúde for indigenous villages; CODEVASF for São Francisco and Parnaíba basins; and Ministério do Meio Ambiente).
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Pages 1-2] Resumo & Section 1; [PDF Pages 6-9] Section 3; [PDF Pages 11-12] Section 4

domain_ratings.justification: Conceptually defines the institutional-legal exposure—decentralized municipal titularity and planning obligations paired with fragmented federal agency mandates and fiscal-borrowing constraints—clearly in qualitative policy terms, though not operationalized as a formal quantitative treatment variable.

Identifies concrete sectoral governance and service outcomes (state household sanitation coverage, presence of municipal sanitation/solid-waste plans, councils, and funds, deadline extensions, federal program counts, and federal budget allocations), though Gráfico 2 conflates PNRS solid-waste instruments with basic sanitation planning discussed in the text and precise indicator formulas are omitted.

No dedicated methods section defines sampling frames, time horizons, or inclusion rules for literature, official reports, or administrative records; PDF p. 6 cites a 2017 survey of 3,905 municipalities while PDF p. 12 cites 5,570 total municipalities without explaining sample coverage or missingness.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Pages 1-3] Resumo & Section 1; [PDF Page 6] Section 3; [PDF Page 12] Section 4

domain_ratings.justification: Literature, statutes, audit reports, and descriptive charts are selected purposively to illustrate federative asymmetries without a documented search strategy, screening criteria, or safeguards against selective evidence inclusion.

While administrative data sources are named (SNIS 2017, SIGA Brasil, SIGPLAN/ME, SIOP 2020), the article does not specify SNIS indicator codes, SIOP budget functions/subfunctions, whether 2015-2019 budget figures are nominal or inflation-adjusted, or how federal sanitation programs were counted.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Pages 6-9] Section 3 (Gráficos 1-3); [PDF Page 11] Section 4 (Gráfico 4); [PDF Pages 13-14] Section 5

domain_ratings.justification: Relies entirely on narrative institutional analysis and univariate/bivariate descriptive administrative summaries without any counterfactual design, comparative control group, or statistical modeling to identify causal effects of federalist legal arrangements on municipal sanitation deficits.

Major structural confounders—small population size, low local tax capacity, rural isolation, low human development, and national fiscal contraction—are recognized in the narrative text via secondary sources (e.g., IPEA 2010; Mendes 2012), but there is no empirical adjustment or stratification isolating institutional design from socioeconomic capacity.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Pages 3, 5] Section 2; [PDF Pages 7-8] Section 3; [PDF Pages 10-12] Section 4

domain_ratings.justification: Provides a rich, well-informed institutional account of Brazilian intergovernmental relations, covering FPM transfer dependence, electoral disincentives for high-O&M network investments, overlapping mandates across five federal agencies, TCU oversight pressures, inter-municipal consortia rules, and failed capacity-building efforts (GESPÚBLICA / Núcleo Setorial Saneamento).

Although underlying federal portals (SNIS, SIOP, SIGA Brasil) are publicly accessible, exact replication is hindered by omitted query dates/parameters (beyond a generic April 1, 2020 access date for SIOP), unspecified budget rubrics, unnumbered federal decrees in Figura 1, and absence of tabular numerical values in the text.

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not applicable / Can't tell: No longitudinal cohort or panel tracking of units over time; however, substantial unaddressed municipal non-coverage/non-response exists in the cited 2017 municipal sanitation plan survey (3,905 municipalities surveyed out of 5,570 total Brazilian municipalities).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern: Structural confounders—municipal population size, rural isolation, low human development, weak local tax bases, and macroeconomic fiscal crisis—are discussed narratively via secondary literature, but no statistical, design-based, or comparative controls isolate federalist legal-institutional effects from socioeconomic determinants.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate: Core constitutional, statutory, and regulatory instruments (1988 Federal Constitution Art. 23, Law 11.445/2007, Law 11.107/2005, EC 95/2016, Portaria 171/2014 PLANSAB, Portaria 141/2005, MP 868/2018, PL 4.162/2019) and federal agency mandates are substantively described, though minor statutory citation slips appear (e.g., 'Lei n. 11.447/2007' on PDF p. 11) and specific decree numbers postponing municipal planning deadlines are omitted in Figura 1 and the reference list.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern: Secondary administrative metrics from SNIS (2017), SIGA Brasil/SIGPLAN, and SIOP (2020) are presented in high-level charts without variable codes, budget rubric definitions, price deflation details (nominal vs. real expenditure in Gráfico 4), or data validation; Gráfico 2 labels solid-waste (PNRS) instruments while the text discusses basic sanitation plans, and the author cites Nirazawa and Oliveira (2018) regarding municipal sanitation data unreliability.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak: Outcomes (state-level treated sewage coverage, municipal management instruments, federal program proliferation, and 2015-2019 budget trends) rely on unvalidated secondary administrative aggregates without underlying numerical tables, indicator formulas, or adjustment for incomplete municipal reporting.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: High concern: No research protocol, pre-specified indicator set, or systematic search/selection strategy is reported; administrative series, audit findings, and secondary studies are selectively marshaled to support the narrative argument.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern: Purposive, non-systematic selection of literature, official documents, and descriptive administrative data years (SNIS 2017; SIOP 2015-2019), alongside unexamined municipal coverage gaps (3,905 surveyed vs. 5,570 total municipalities in SNIS).

overall_narrative_summary: This article is a doctrinal-institutional and descriptive secondary-data case study examining how Brazil's post-1988 federative architecture, fragmented federal agency mandates, and fiscal-regulatory rules constrain municipal implementation of basic sanitation policy. Appraised under the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework (structured non-validated judgment), its principal strengths lie in jurisdictional specificity (D2: strong) and institutional contextualization (D10: strong), alongside adequate legal source identification (D1: adequate, noting minor statutory citation typos and unnumbered federal decrees in Figura 1) and conceptual exposure/outcome framing (D3, D4: adequate). Conversely, empirical and methodological transparency is weak across sampling (D5), source/data selection (D6), indicator and budget measurement reporting (D7), causal identification (D8), confounding control (D9), replication potential (D11), coding rules (D12), and researcher reflexivity (D13). Descriptive charts from SNIS (2017), SIGA Brasil/SIGPLAN, and SIOP (2015-2019) illustrate structural disparities and federal fragmentation, but cannot support causal inference separating legal-institutional design from underlying municipal fiscal and socioeconomic constraints.
where_found_summary: Methods statement in Resumo ([PDF Page 1]) and Section 1 Introdução ([PDF Pages 2-3]); theoretical federalism review in Section 2 ([PDF Pages 3-5]); statutory definitions, SNIS 2017 descriptive charts, deadline-postponement flowchart, and federal agency mapping in Section 3 ([PDF Pages 5-10]); fiscal rules, PL 4.162/2019 regulatory analysis, SIOP 2015-2019 budget chart, TCU oversight, and capacity-building discussion in Section 4 ([PDF Pages 10-13]); policy recommendations and data limitation caveats in Section 5 ([PDF Pages 13-15]); legal and secondary references in Referências ([PDF Pages 15-16]).
